claims.text: Form is the kind of text a piece is, such as an article, a speech, an email or a review, together with the conventions its readers expect of that kind.

claims.text: Conventions are the features readers expect of a form, such as a headline in an article or a salutation in a letter; a writer can follow them or break them deliberately.

claims.text: Every convention does a job for the reader: a headline lets a reader decide quickly whether to read on, a salutation shows who is addressed. An analysis names the job, not just the convention.

verification.method: Authored originally for the YYeni 9093 AS build under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Each form the papers use has its own set of conventions: an article carries a headline, a standfirst, a byline, quoted voices and short paragraphs; a speech addresses its audience directly, signposts its route, repeats key points for listeners and closes memorably; a formal letter and an email open with a salutation, state their purpose early and sign off; a blog uses a personal voice, direct address, headings and an invitation to respond; a review states what is reviewed, judges it against criteria, gives evidence and a verdict; a diary or memoir writes in the first person and sets reflection beside events; a leaflet, brochure or advertisement uses headings, direct address, imperatives, benefits and a call to action; a report has a title, a stated purpose, findings in sections, recommendations and an impersonal register; a podcast or scripted talk keeps a host’s voice, spoken markers and signposting for listeners.

verification.method: Authored originally for the YYeni 9093 AS build under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Naming a form’s conventions is not analysing them: a convention counts in an analysis only when the writer says what job it does for this reader.

verification.method: Authored originally for the YYeni 9093 AS build under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An unseen text’s form is identified from five kinds of evidence: its layout, who it addresses, the voice it uses, its register, and what it is for.
